p.x:
I live with my mum, my dad and my little brother. My dad is a great father. He works in an office, but he always comes home early to play with us. My mum is a doctor, and she is very busy.
My parents have one son and one daughter: my brother and me! My brother is five, and he's a funny kid. Every night at bedtime, my dad reads us a story.
My mum says being a parent is the hardest job in the world, but also the best. I think my parents are the best mum and dad ever.

When my sister had her first baby, everything changed. A newborn needs care 24 hours a day. My sister and her husband had many sleepless nights, feeding the baby and changing nappies.
They bought a cot, a pram and lots of tiny clothes. Every night, my sister sang a lullaby until the baby fell asleep. Her husband took two weeks of paternity leave, and she had three months of maternity leave from work.
When the baby was older, they had to think about childcare. Some parents send their children to daycare, while others hire a nanny. On special evenings, they sometimes use a babysitter.
Now my nephew is four. My sister says the most important thing in parenting is to spend quality time together. She tries to praise him when he's good and to use rewards like stickers rather than punish him. She wants to bring up a well-behaved child who obeys important rules but also feels loved. 'He needs to understand the consequences of his actions,' she says. Being a single parent, she adds, would be even harder.

p.t: What Kind of Parent Are You?
p.x:
Psychologists have long tried to identify which parenting styles produce the happiest and most successful children. One influential model describes three main approaches. Authoritarian parents set strict rules and expect obedience without question. Permissive parents, by contrast, are warm but lenient, rarely setting limits. Between the two lies the authoritative style, which combines clear rules with warmth, explanation and respect for the child's views. Research consistently links this third style with confident, well-adjusted children.
In recent years, new labels have appeared. The helicopter parent hovers over every aspect of a child's life, while the tiger parent pushes children relentlessly towards academic success. In reaction, some families have embraced free-range parenting, giving children the freedom to play and travel independently.
Family structure also matters. Psychologists have long debated whether birth order influences personality, with eldest children sometimes described as responsible and youngest as sociable, although the evidence is mixed. Sibling rivalry, competition between brothers and sisters for attention, is common and usually harmless.
Modern economic realities add pressure. In many families, both adults are working parents, and the cost of childcare can be enormous. Some couples decide that one partner will become a stay-at-home parent, while others struggle to balance careers and family. Many parents report feelings of guilt, worrying that they are not spending enough time with their children. Experts reassure them that there is no perfect formula: consistency, affection and genuine interest in a child's life matter far more than following any single style.
